transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Khan (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (Elysium CTO), Marta Liu (Elysium ML), Omar Reyes (Elysium Infra), Jun Park (Elysium SRE)
Links shared: KV-cache design doc (redwood.com/docs/kv-cache), benchmark spreadsheet (tinyurl.com/elysium-kv-bench), security doc (redwood.com/security.pdf)

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we wanted to dig into the evictions and paging you're seeing with long context workloads, so quick intros?
00:15 Dana Ortiz: Hi I'm Dana, CTO at Elysium, running an internal assistant with 200k monthly active users, largely long docs, so we've been hitting cache thrash.
00:30 Ravi Patel: Cool thanks. From Redwood SE side I'm Ravi, I'll be running the repro and kernel traces.
00:45 Marta Liu: Marta here, i'm the ML eng, we see latency spikes and repeated KV misses after about 8k tokens in the context window.
01:02 Omar Reyes: Omar infra, we've got a VPC setup on GCP, some on-prem for sensitive data, curious about VPC networking and memory constraints.
01:20 Maya Chen: Great, agenda: root cause hypothesis (eviction thresholds/paging), prefix reuse patterns, impact of quantized weights and batching on KV cache, and mitigation + repro plan.

04:40 Ravi Patel: To lay out the basics, the KV cache is per-sequence and we maintain a per-GPU cache shard. Under sustained long-context traffic you can hit two things: either the cache hits capacity and triggers eviction, or we start paging segments to host memory depending on your deployment profile.
05:02 Marta Liu: Is paging to host memory automatic? We're seeing big jitter not just steady latency increases.
05:18 Ravi Patel: In some private/on-prem configs we allow host-side paging to avoid OOM, but that adds a lot of variance. It's not turned on for hosted by default. Sounds like you're on a mix which explains the jitter.
06:00 Jun Park: Can you clarify eviction policy? LRU? MRU? Something custom?
06:20 Ravi Patel: We use a hybrid policy: time-decay + recency weight to favor prefixes that are frequently reused. It's not pure LRU because that punishes high-reuse prefixes. But heavy tail workloads with many unique prefixes will still cause churn.
07:05 Dana Ortiz: Our app has low prefix reuse per user session but lots of cross-session shared prompts. So prefix reuse is intermittent, not per-session.
07:30 Samir Khan: That intermittent reuse is tricky — with interleaved users you get fragmentation in the cache (prefixs scatter). If the cache shard is small the eviction will evict parts of prefixes that are still useful.
08:00 Marta Liu: We also quantize our model to int8 for cost, could that affect KV lengths or evictions?
08:22 Ravi Patel: Quantization affects model weights, not the cache keys per se, but in practice quantized kernels change memory footprints for activations and can change how much KV fits in GPU memory. So yes, switching quantization knobs can indirectly increase eviction frequency.
09:05 Omar Reyes: For our VPC/on-prem nodes we have stricter memory caps — is there a recommended config?
09:20 Ravi Patel: We typically recommend reserving an extra 20-30% headroom for KV-heavy workloads, and enabling shard-level logging so you can monitor active KV sizes. We'll share a config snippet.

12:45 Maya Chen: Let's look at the repro steps you mentioned in your ticket — Marta, you said you can produce a 10k-token prompt set?
13:02 Marta Liu: Yes we've got a set of 50 long prompts (8-12k tokens) and an access pattern that simulates 200 qps with spike bursts. We'll upload the set.
13:30 Ravi Patel: Perfect. For the repro we'll run with: same model variant, quantization profile matched, same batch/latency targets, and capture KV eviction traces + paging counters.

16:10 Dana Ortiz: We observed something we call "prefix fade" — after about 6-8k tokens a previously used prefix becomes a miss even within the same session. Could that be eviction or a bug in prefix matching?
16:35 Ravi Patel: Two possibilities: 1) eviction due to shard compaction, 2) prefix hashing collision / normalization mismatch on your end. We should confirm whether the prefix bytes are identical after tokenization. Sometimes tokenizer mismatch causes apparent misses.
17:05 Marta Liu: Hmm tokenizer mismatch is possible — we run a custom tokenizer variant.
17:22 Samir Khan: If tokenizer differs you'll see different KV keys entirely. We'll add a hash comparator in the repro to validate.
18:00 Jun Park: Also, do we have any metrics for prefix reuse rate? That might clarify whether it's eviction or unique prefix load.
18:18 Ravi Patel: We'll enable per-prefix hit rate telemetry in the test run. Note it adds overhead but fine for repro.

21:40 Omar Reyes: About paging — is there a hybrid approach where hot parts of KV stay pinned and cold pages go to host?
22:05 Ravi Patel: Yeah we support hot-set pinning heuristics. We can mark prefixes as pinned if they exceed reuse thresholds. But that consumes reserved memory. Tradeoff is between hit-rate and increased OOM risk under spike.
22:40 Dana Ortiz: How do you decide reuse thresholds? Tunable?
22:55 Ravi Patel: Tunable. We'll start with defaults tuned for web-scale chat, but for your workload with long docs we recommend lowering the eviction aggressiveness and increasing pinned-set size. We'll show the config diff.

26:10 Marta Liu: On batching — does larger batching help overall throughput but worsen latency tails due to sequential dependency?
26:30 Samir Khan: Exactly. Batching increases throughput and amortizes KV lookups, but it raises p99 latency because you wait to fill batches. For low-latency long-context queries you probably want smaller batches and more aggressive async prefix prefetching.
27:05 Ravi Patel: Also continuous batching with dynamic deadlines can help — it lets critical requests bypass batching under tight latency SLOs.

30:00 Dana Ortiz: Any known interactions between quantization and cache consistency? We've seen slightly different generations when using int8 and fp16 variants.
30:20 Ravi Patel: The model's numerical differences can result in different tokenization decision boundaries in edge cases, which changes subsequent tokens and therefore downstream cache keys. It's subtle but can manifest as divergence in repeated prompts when switching quantization. So keep model variant pinned for bench runs.
31:00 Marta Liu: Good to know. We'll pin the variant.

33:45 Maya Chen: We also wanted to mention prefix reuse across users — some apps share system prompts widely, that should be pinned globally to improve hit rate. That requires a global policy and isn't default for per-tenant isolation.
34:10 Omar Reyes: We have multi-tenant groups, can we configure cross-tenant pinned prefixes?
34:28 Ravi Patel: In Dedicated you can choose shared cache pools or strict per-tenant isolation. Shared improves global reuse but has security/isolation tradeoffs. For Elysium, maybe run a hybrid: shared for non-sensitive system prompts, per-tenant for user data.

37:55 Marta Liu: If we run the repro and see sustained paging, what's the typical mitigation path? More GPUs or change eviction/pinning?
38:10 Samir Khan: Start with config: increase pinning for hot prefixes, increase headroom memory, reduce batch size for latency-critical calls. If still insufficient, scale horizontal shards (more GPUs) to increase aggregate KV capacity.
38:30 Dana Ortiz: Any impact on cost when scaling shards? We need rough numbers.
38:45 Maya Chen: We'll include cost delta estimates in the follow-up doc — e.g., add 1-2 GPUs reduces eviction but increases cost by X% depending on instance type.

41:15 Jun Park: About tracing and logs: what counters should we capture?
41:28 Ravi Patel: Eviction count, paging in/out, per-prefix hit rate, shard utilization, tail-latency distribution, kernel time per token, and GPU memory headroom. We'll provide a logging template.

44:00 Dana Ortiz: One more question — we've seen prefix reuse degraded after a hot restart. Could there be cache warming issues?
44:20 Ravi Patel: Yep, on restarts the cache is empty. We support warm-starting from persisted KV snapshots for dedicated/private deployments, but snapshotting size depends on your persistence policy. Snapshots reduce cold-start misses.
44:50 Marta Liu: Do you recommend snapshot frequency?
44:58 Ravi Patel: Depends on churn; for high reuse apps daily snapshots + warm-up replay of top prefixes on startup works. We'll share recommended cron and snapshot restore hints.

47:10 Maya Chen: OK quick recap — we will: 1) provision dedicated repro cluster, 2) run eviction + paging traces with your long-context prompts, 3) enable per-prefix telemetry and tokenization hash comparator, 4) test configs: default, increased pinning, and increased memory headroom.
47:40 Dana Ortiz: Sounds good. Who's owner on the repro?
47:48 Ravi Patel: I'll own the repro and data collection.
48:00 Maya Chen: Maya to follow up on docs and schedule.

51:15 Marta Liu: A couple minor things — one of our engineers noticed KV keys with slightly different whitespace normalized tokenization, likely our tokenizer variant. We'll standardize for the repro.
51:40 Samir Khan: Good call. Also watch for collisions if you do any custom hashing — the comparator will help.

55:00 Dana Ortiz: Thanks everyone — valuable session. We'll expect the repro results next week and then reconvene.
55:20 Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll get artifacts over.
55:30 Meeting end."
